title.narrative: Mobility and Needs Monitoring – Displacement Tracking Matrix for Syrian Arab Republic

description.narrative: The protracted conflict in Syria has led to a severe lack of security in many areas, further exacerbated by both economic and humanitarian crises. On top of this, the absence of basic services has significantly heightened people’s vulnerabilities, particularly for those most in need. Without immediate support from the government and humanitarian partners, vital services such as water, sanitation, healthcare, electricity, and education will continue to worsen, pushing more people into extreme hardship. Furthermore, increasing the risk of harmful coping mechanisms and hindering the return of internally displaced persons (IDPs) and refugees, or those in secondary displacement. Investing in these essential services is critical to create a more sustainable response, avert new crises, and support those who have already begun returning. IDPs, returnees and host communities, require urgent humanitarian assistance, including food, shelter, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), and protection. Additionally, those seeking refuge in and out of camps and informal sites face heightened protection risks, such as inadequate privacy, limited access to basic services, increased vulnerability to gender-based violence (GBV), and potential health risks due to overcrowding. Furthermore, displacement takes a toll on the psychosocial well-being of all IDPs, affecting both adults and children. Currently, one of the main challenges for the humanitarian community are the significant data gaps inside Syria due to the prior conflicts and ongoing displacement since 2011 and the limited access provided by the Government of Syria over the last 13 years; which further complicates the effective provision of essential lifesaving services by humanitarian partners. While there have been efforts to collect data, especially in non-government-controlled areas, challenges remain in obtaining comprehensive and up-to-date information covering all 14 governorates inside Syria. The recent changes in the political situation have further resulted in increasing mobility dynamics, which underpins the need for a proper evidence base programming, allowing all actors to gain a full understanding of the situation and appropriately adapt their respective responses. As a response, an integrated, multi-sectoral, participatory, and flexible approach is therefore required to address the complex issues resulting from short to medium-term forced displacement, IDP returns and provide lifesaving assistance. Building on its existing programmes and field presence, IOM through CERF is proposing to contribute to a comprehensive and integrated humanitarian intervention, allowing the most urgent and pressing needs to be addressed swiftly by providing evidence base to guide responses. The main objective is to ensure dignified, safe, and secure living conditions, along with basic services for vulnerable populations affected by the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Syria. IOM thus proposed a twofold response including I) Country-wide needs identification, including in hard-to-reach areas); and II) Well-coordinated multisectoral response by OCHA and partners to support the most vulnerable conflict affected populations. IOM’s approach will be guided by data and tools stemming from IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM)’s effective operational capacity for data collection, ultimately leading to a countrywide comprehensive multi-sectoral needs assessment. This data-driven approach will enable IOM and all humanitarian partners to identify areas where vulnerable populations are concentrated, allowing for a better understanding of the specific challenges these groups face, including geographical and sectoral targeted responses, aimed at the most vulnerable groups. (Remaining part of Summary in comments)
